{{Short description|Type of Japanese shrines}}

[[File:IseShrineBuilding.jpg|thumb|275x275px|A building at Ise Shrine]]
'''Shinmei shrines''' ({{Langx|ja|神明神社|lit=Shrine of deity}}) are [[Shinto shrine|shrines]] dedicated to the worship of the Japanese solar deity [[Amaterasu]]. The head Shinmei shrine is [[Ise Grand Shrine]] which inspired the [[Shinmei-zukuri]] architectural style.

== History ==
The solar goddess of [[Shinto]], [[Amaterasu Omikami]], is considered to be the ancestral deity of the [[Imperial House of Japan]], and is widely worshiped in agricultural rituals. During the [[Kofun period|Kofun Period]], a number of Shinmei Shrines, such as [[Ise Grand Shrine]], were constructed and dedicated to Amaterasu. In national rituals, only the [[Emperor of Japan|emperor]] was permitted to make offerings towards the deity.<ref>Nishigaki 1983, p.28</ref>

However, as the power of the imperial court declined in the middle of the [[Heian period|Heian Period]], the central government could no longer financially support the Shinmei Shrines. As a result, the responsibilities of their maintenance fell onto local feudal lords, who were also given the right to relay prayers. Local lords donated part of their own estates ([[Shōen]]) as Shinryo ({{Langx|ja|神領|lit=Domain of gods}}) to construct shrines dedicated to Amaterasu, including [[Nishina Shinmei Shrine]] in [[Ōmachi, Nagano|Ōmachi]], Shinmei Shrine in [[Yokohama]], and Amatsu Shinmei Shrine in [[Kamogawa, Chiba|Kamogawa]]. Some of the Shinmei Shrines, such as the Shiba Great Shrine, were said to have predated the Shōen System.<ref>Kawamori 1985, pp.80-83</ref>

The priests of Shinmei Shrines, also known as Oshi ({{Langx|ja|御師|lit=Royal teacher}}), temporarily enshrined the talisman [[Jingū taima|Jingū Taima]] in their branch offices in the eastern part of Japan, and some of these offices later developed into Shinmei Shrines as well.<ref>Nishigaki 1983, pp.162-164</ref>

During the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] and later [[Muromachi period|Muromachi Periods]], Oshi's influence began to spread among both high-ranking samurai class and the common people.<ref>Nishigaki 1983, p.114</ref> Especially in [[Kyoto]], an increasing number of shrines outside of the traditional Shinryo were given permission by Oshi to enshrine Amaterasu. These shrines came to be known as "Imashinmei" ({{Langx|ja|今神明|lit=Current Shinmei}}) or "Hishinmei" ({{Langx|ja|飛神明|lit=Flying Shinmei}}).<ref>Seta 1985, pp.290-291</ref> In the [[Edo period|Edo Period]], the Ise faith became even more popular, spreading throughout the country and permeating a wide range of social classes.<ref>Shinjo 1949, p.144</ref> In 1632, Ise Shrine published the Ise Calendar in 1632, which recorded dates for agricultural activities and was widely used before the [[Meiji Restoration]].<ref>Nishigaki 1983, pp.156-157</ref> As the influence of Ise Shrine and its deity Amaterasu grew, the number of Shinmei Shrines increased further.
